geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the intended region: it shades the two subregions between the lower lines y=-x+1 and y=x+1 and the top boundary y=3 over x=-2..0 and x=0..2, with the correct V-shaped lower boundary, top segment, vertical slices, and R₁/R₂ decomposition. geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the unit-cell geometry because it preserves the correct relative lattice parameters for SC, BCC, and FCC with a constant atom radius, places the correct numbers of corner/body/face atoms, and uses an oblique textbook-style stacked layout for lattice-point and sphere unit-cell views. Figure 2 has the correct atom counts and local packing relationships, but it normalizes all cubes to the same edge length by scaling atom radii, loses the cross-structure proportions, and arranges the two models diagonally side-by-side with a generic isometric view rather than matching the likely source layout and projection.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 handles the requested interactions more completely: its structure buttons update both the lattice diagram and space-filling model, reset the selection state, update the active button and label, and clicking an atom produces an in-figure readout with the correct fractional contribution and total atom count formula. Figure 2’s toggle mostly works, but its click feedback is only through the scaffold popup rather than a visible in-figure readout and it gives much less counting detail. Both figures have a correctness flaw because hidden atoms remain registered/raycastable after toggling, so clicks in empty or hidden-atom locations can report atoms that are not currently drawn; this is especially problematic, but Figure 1 still provides the stronger and more complete intended interaction when visible atoms are clicked.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the recognizable cube perspective for the lattice-point diagram and a simple-cubic unit-cell rendering with grey corner spheres, translucent green cube, and matching labels. Figure 2 shows the lattice locations as a flattened hexagonal/diagonal network rather than the textbook cube, and its unit-cell title/label overlap the geometry, making the composition less like the original.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the main labels from the reference for the visible simple-cubic view placed more readably: “Lattice point locations,” “Cubic unit cells,” and “Simple cubic” are mostly clear and not colliding with the artwork. Figure 2 includes similar label text, but the labels overlap or sit directly on the diagrams and spheres, especially “Cubic unit cells” and “Simple cubic,” making them cluttered and harder to read. Both figures miss the full set of reference labels for the body-centered and face-centered examples in the rendered view and include extra UI text, but Figure 1’s label placement and readability are noticeably better.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 represents the core chemistry more faithfully: its top diagrams place black corner lattice points and the correct red body- or face-centered lattice points, and its bottom models use space-filling spheres with the correct contacts for SC, BCC, and FCC while also giving correct fractional atom counts (L00014, L00016, L00018-L00019). Figure 2 gets the same basic lattice-point locations and contact relationships mostly right, but it keeps the cube edge fixed and rescales atom radii between structures, which is a less faithful way to teach the packing geometry and may imply that the structure change is primarily a change in atom size rather than in the unit-cell geometry; it also does less to make the atom-counting framework explicit than Figure 1 (L00018-L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger across all dimensions: it preserves the textbook-like cube perspective and relative SC/BCC/FCC unit-cell geometry with constant atom radius, uses clearer non-overlapping labels, and provides more complete in-figure interaction feedback including fractional atom-count formulas. Figure 2 has the basic lattice locations and some working toggles, but it normalizes cube sizes by rescaling atoms, has cluttered/overlapping labels and a less faithful flattened layout, and gives weaker click/counting feedback; both have a hidden-atom clickability flaw, but Figure 1 remains more accurate and complete overall.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook structure by preserving the three sequential vial/molecular snapshots above a concentration-time graph, with two opposing concentration curves, a dashed equilibrium marker, shaded equilibrium region, axis arrows, and panel labels. Figure 2 instead merges a single molecular container into the plotting coordinate system, uses an artificial negative x-domain to make room for it, omits the three-time-point vial layout and panel structure, and its graph/rate scaling and axis layout are less faithful to the expected 2D structure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the advertised time interaction more correctly: the marker can actually be dragged, the time slider and drag update the molecular/tube view, readouts, and curves together, and the concentration/rate mode switch recomputes and redraws the appropriate graph. Figure 1’s sliders and toggle mostly work, but it claims the time marker can be dragged while the graph marker itself only shows a popup, its readout shows either concentrations or rates rather than both simultaneously, and repeated redraws leave stale duplicated panel labels; its initial-concentration updates also do not consistently update the equilibrium tube color as an absolute color change.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook figure because it preserves the three molecular snapshots across the top, the labeled concentration-time graph with red and blue curves, the equilibrium shading, dashed vertical line, and panel labeling. Figure 2 captures some chemistry and curve colors, but its layout is substantially different, with only one large molecular container beside the graph, added legend/tooltip elements, and a composition that no longer resembles the original multipanel textbook figure as closely.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has substantially better label fidelity to the original: it includes the top labels “t = 0,” “pre-equilibrium,” and “at equilibrium,” the species labels N2O4 and NO2, panel markers, axis labels, and the “Equilibrium achieved” annotation. Figure 2 omits most of the original textbook labels and annotations, replaces them with a legend, tooltip, numeric axes, and interface text, and lacks the multi-panel labeling structure, so its labels match the original much less well despite some readable text.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the reversible elementary reaction: its concentrations are generated from the mass-action forward and reverse rates, so [N₂O₄] falls, [NO₂] rises, the forward rate k_f[N₂O₄] decreases, and the reverse rate k_r[NO₂]² increases until the rates match at equilibrium, which directly supports the concepts in the brief (L00012, L00020-L00023). Figure 2 captures the same qualitative trends, but its concentration curves are imposed as a simple exponential approach rather than being dynamically consistent with the stated rate laws, and its shaded “equilibrium achieved” point is only approximate, so the relationship between the concentration curves and the equal-rate condition is less conceptually faithful (L00012, L00023).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it preserves the textbook’s three-stage molecular snapshots, panel structure, original labels, concentration-time graph, equilibrium marker, and the chemically consistent relationship between concentration changes and equal forward/reverse rates. Figure 2 has better implemented time dragging and coordinated controls, but relative to Figure 1 it substantially departs from the source layout, omits many original labels and annotations, and uses less dynamically faithful concentration curves.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 reconstructs the intended geometry much more accurately: it uses a 6-channel by 7-height by 6-width input slab with channels receding in depth, a receptive field spanning all channels with adjustable kernel width, six weight cubes in a row, and an output slab whose valid width shrinks as expected. Figure 2 has noticeably wrong element counts and spatial relationships, including a 6×6×7 input arrangement, only four output channels, a large 6×4×3 block of weights instead of six filter cubes, and axes/flow geometry that do not match the intended compact textbook layout.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2’s controls more correctly update the quantities they advertise: the output-channel slider changes the highlighted output channel, emphasizes the corresponding row/slice of the weight tensor, and redraws contribution arrows from all input channels, while its kernel-width slider changes the visible kernel offsets, receptive-field span, and output width. Figure 1’s sliders function without obvious breakage and handle a wider kernel range, but its weight tensor is only a row of cubes that does not change with kernel width and only loosely represents the selected filter slice or per-input-channel contributions, so the advertised interactions are less semantically correct.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the reference composition: a dense input layer of circles with width/height/channel annotations, a grey horizontal receptive field, a short row of colored weight blocks, and a smaller output layer with one highlighted unit. Figure 2 has the same broad topic, but the weights are rendered as a large stacked grid of cubes with extra outlines and connection arrows, which makes the central geometry and overall resemblance noticeably less like the textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the main textbook labels present and mostly correct, including “Channels,” “Width,” “Height,” “Input layer, H,” “Weights, Ω,” and “Output layer, H′,” with readable placement relative to the diagram. Figure 2 uses an incorrect singular “Channel,” places it awkwardly inside/overlapping the input stack, has smaller/lighter labels that are harder to read, and the central annotations are more cluttered around the weights; both include extra UI labels not in the original, but Figure 1’s actual diagram labels match the reference better.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 is conceptually more accurate because its Ω object is a genuine 3D weight tensor indexed by input channel, output channel, and kernel offset, matching the multi-channel convolution idea of a weighted linear combination across channel and spatial dimensions (L00007). Figure 1 instead represents Ω as only a row of six cubes, with each cube treated as an entire output-channel filter, which collapses the actual tensor structure and weakens or misstates how individual weights connect input channels and kernel positions to an output channel (L00007). Both figures show input/output channel volumes, axes, convolution/bias operators, and valid-width shrinkage, but Figure 2 better preserves the relationship between input channels, kernel width, output channels, and individual weights, whereas Figure 1 mostly illustrates output-channel selection rather than the full multi-channel convolution tensor.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it more accurately matches the intended textbook composition and geometry, with the correct input/output slab structure, receptive-field placement, valid-width shrinkage, and clearer labels such as Channels, Width, Height, Weights Ω, and Output layer H′. Figure 2 has a more semantically meaningful weight tensor and better slider behavior, but relative to Figure 1 it introduces incorrect element counts, a less faithful central weight layout, cluttered arrows, weaker label placement, and an overall geometry that departs more from the reference.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the working U-Net topology with a complete left-to-right chain of 3D blocks, functional skip arrows spanning encoder to decoder stages, labels, flow arrows, and time-embedding branches. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 clearly resembles the reference U-Net-style architecture with orange encoder/decoder blocks, skip-connection arrows labeled Concatenate, shape labels, noisy image planes, and time-embedding arrows, even though it is compressed and partially obscured by the interface. Figure 2 fails visually because the actual diagram is essentially absent from the screenshot, leaving mostly blank space and controls, so it is not recognizable as the textbook figure.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more truthfully represents the requested diffusion U-Net: it instantiates the specified encoder resolution sequence and a mirrored decoder back to the output, with skip connections labeled “Concatenate,” a circled t feeding a bottom time-embedding path, and a legend distinguishing residual blocks from residual blocks with self-attention (L00007). aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall result because it visibly presents a recognizable U-Net-style architecture with encoder/decoder blocks, skip connections, labels, time-embedding arrows, and a coherent left-to-right topology, while Figure 2’s rendered diagram is largely absent and its skip-connection geometry is broken despite some stronger source-level intent. Figure 2 has better-functioning controls and a conceptually cleaner encoded resolution sequence, but those advantages are outweighed by its failure to display the main architectural content that Figure 1 mostly preserves.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more recognizable as the original labeled panel a: it preserves the left-to-right network layout, orange bias connections, black input-to-hidden edges, gray hidden-to-output labels, θ/φ notation, panel label, and similar node composition.
